meaning: A long pointed piece of ice hanging down
trick: ICE + CYCLE: water drips, freezes, drips again.
examples: If you fling snot in Siberia, it's a green icicle before it hits the ground.
An icicle hung from the edge of the roof.

meaning: Long pointed pieces of ice hanging down
trick: ICE + CYCLES: drip, freeze, repeat.
examples: Icicles hung like crystals from the edges of the houses.
Icicles formed on the trees overnight.

meaning: In a very cold, unfriendly way
trick: ICE + -LY: looking at you like ice.
examples: He stood at the top of the stairs, looking down icily on the crowd.
"No, thank you," she said icily.

meaning: Very unfriendly and cold in manner; also extremely cold or covered with ice
trick: ICY like ice - a cold welcome freezes you out.
examples: Our icy reception told us we had to go another way.
She gave me an icy look when I came in late.

usage.pattern: an icy + noun / be icy towards someone

meaning: Very stupid or silly
trick: IDIOT + -IC: what an idiot would do.
examples: "It's idiotic," she said, shaking her head.
It was idiotic to drive without a seatbelt.

usage.pattern: be idiotic to do something / an idiotic + noun

meaning: Without doing anything useful or without a purpose; (of an engine) running slowly while not moving
trick: IDLE + -LY: sitting idle, doing nothing.
examples: She watched the buses growling idly at the curb.
He sat idly flipping through the TV channels.

usage.pattern: do something idly / sit idly by

meaning: The worship of idols or images as gods; also too much love or admiration for someone
trick: IDOL + -ATRY (worship): idol-worship.
examples: The Taliban blew up the Buddhas, calling them objects of idolatry.
Some religions strictly forbid idolatry.

usage.pattern: idolatry of something / an act of idolatry

meaning: Causing public shame or embarrassment
trick: IGNOMINIOUS - 'ignore my name': so shameful you want your name forgotten.
examples: Within five minutes they were in ignominious retreat, with geese hissing after them.
The team suffered an ignominious defeat at home.

meaning: Not knowing about something; also lacking knowledge or education in general
trick: IGNORE-ant: an ant that ignores everything knows nothing.
examples: The child grew up ignorant of the cruelties of life.
I was ignorant of the new rules until today.

meaning: (of clothes) not the right size or shape for the person wearing them
trick: ILL (bad) + FITTING: a bad fit.
examples: She would wear an ill-fitting gray shirt buttoned to the throat.
He looked uncomfortable in his ill-fitting suit.

meaning: Born to parents who are not married to each other; also not allowed by law or rules
trick: IL (not) + LEGITIMATE: not legitimate.
examples: Mariam was an illegitimate child who never felt she belonged.
The election result was called illegitimate by the opposition.

meaning: Felt or done secretly because it is not allowed; also illegal
trick: ILLICIT sounds like ILLEGAL - both are 'ill' for the law.
examples: Her satisfaction from the outburst felt meager, somehow illicit.
Police found illicit drugs in the car.

meaning: To make something clear or easier to understand; also to light up
trick: ILLUMINATE has LUMEN (light): shine light on an idea.
examples: This story will illuminate a proven path to self-mastery.
The teacher used a simple example to illuminate the idea.

meaning: Perfectly clean and tidy; also without any mistakes
trick: IM (not) + MACULA (spot): not a single spot.
examples: He pointed to a file on his otherwise immaculate desk.
Her kitchen is always immaculate.

meaning: Extremely large or great
trick: IM (not) + MENSE (measure): too big to measure.
examples: The week stood like an immense, immovable object between her and his next visit.
The project needs an immense amount of work.

meaning: Likely to happen very soon
trick: IMMINENT - it's 'in a minute': about to happen.
examples: Collapse was imminent.
Dark clouds warned that rain was imminent.

meaning: Made unable to move or work normally
trick: IM (not) + MOBILE: made not mobile.
examples: He was immobilized by his bad back.
The heavy snow immobilized the whole city.

usage.pattern: be immobilized by something / immobilize something

meaning: Not affected or harmed by something; also protected from a disease
trick: IMMUNE system - protects you so nothing gets in.
examples: I needed to convince myself I was immune to suffering.
He seems immune to criticism.

meaning: Passed on (knowledge, a quality or a problem) to someone
trick: IMPART = give a PART of yourself to someone.
examples: My parents imparted some of their problems to me.
The old teacher imparted his wisdom to his students.

meaning: Without showing any feeling
trick: IM (not) + PASSION: looking on without passion.
examples: Old vendors gazed at her impassively behind pyramids of cherries.
The guard stared impassively ahead.

meaning: Something that blocks or slows progress; also a problem that makes speaking difficult
trick: IMPEDE + -MENT: your 'ped' (foot) gets stuck.
examples: Love was once seen as an impediment to more important things in life.
Lack of money is the main impediment to growth.

meaning: Delaying or stopping the progress of something
trick: IMPEDE - 'ped' = foot: putting a foot in the way.
examples: A governor is impeding us from reaching our maximum speed.
Fallen trees are impeding traffic on the road.

usage.pattern: impede someone/something / impede someone from doing something

meaning: Impossible to get through or into; also impossible to understand
trick: IM (not) + PENETRABLE: nothing can get through.
examples: The tides are furious against the impenetrable walls.
The forest was thick and impenetrable.

usage.pattern: an impenetrable + noun / impenetrable to something

meaning: Extremely important and needing to be done; also a command
trick: IMPERATIVE - like an EMPEROR's order: must be done.
examples: It was imperative to move beyond doubt.
It is imperative that you arrive on time.

usage.pattern: it is imperative to do something / that ...

meaning: In a way that is too small or slow to be noticed
trick: IM (not) + PERCEPTIBLY: too slight to perceive.
examples: The street grew emptier, almost imperceptibly.
The light changed imperceptibly as evening came.

meaning: Lasting forever; never dying or decaying
trick: IM (not) + PERISHABLE: will never perish.
examples: Their hearts swelled with imperishable pride.
Great art gives its creator imperishable fame.

meaning: Not letting liquid or gas pass through
trick: IM (not) + PERMEABLE: water can't permeate it.
examples: The house has an elegant but impermeable roof.
This jacket is made of impermeable fabric.

meaning: Not affected or influenced by something; also not letting water through
trick: IMPERVIOUS - 'impossible to pierce': nothing gets through.
examples: Entitlement is impervious to criticism.
He seemed impervious to the cold.

meaning: Something that encourages a process or activity to happen
trick: IMPETUS - 'impel-us': what pushes us forward.
examples: The impetus for this transformation was an eighteen-year-old boy.
The new coach gave the team fresh impetus.

usage.pattern: the impetus for something / give impetus to something

meaning: Playfully naughty
trick: IMP (a little devil) + -ISH: like a little imp.
examples: She flashed an impish grin and nudged Laila with an elbow.
The boy had an impish sense of humour.

meaning: Impossible to stop, calm or satisfy
trick: IM (not) + PLACATE: can't be calmed down.
examples: Prisoners rarely escape the implacable machinery of justice.
She faced an implacable enemy.

meaning: Suggested without being said directly
trick: IMPLIED - not 'applied' openly; hinted under the surface.
examples: My wife had given me an implied ultimatum.
There was an implied threat in his words.

usage.pattern: an implied + noun / implied by something

meaning: Begged someone urgently to do something
trick: IMPLORE - 'implore' on the floor: begging on your knees.
examples: The Stoics implored people to keep death in mind at all times.
She implored him to stay.

meaning: Begging urgently and emotionally
trick: IMPLORING on the floor: begging on your knees.
examples: Mariam was screaming and imploring Rasheed to stop.
He gave her an imploring look.

usage.pattern: implore someone to do something / an imploring + noun

meaning: To suggest something without saying it directly; also to have as a necessary result
trick: IMPLY = put IN-PLY: fold a meaning inside the words.
examples: Needs imply survival, the very minimum required to make us act.
Are you implying that I lied?

meaning: Impressive because of large size or appearance
trick: IMPOSING - so big it imposes itself on you.
examples: They marvelled that they had built anything so imposing.
An imposing gate stood at the palace entrance.

meaning: Unable to take effective action; also (of a man) unable to have sex
trick: IM (not) + POTENT (powerful): no power.
examples: She trembled with resentment and impotent rage.
The police felt impotent against the gangs.

usage.pattern: impotent rage / be impotent against something

meaning: Not likely to happen or be true
trick: IM (not) + PROBABLE: not likely.
examples: My goal, however improbable, was not impossible.
It seems improbable that he will win.

usage.pattern: it is improbable that ... / an improbable + noun

meaning: Lack of care or good judgement about risks
trick: IM (not) + PRUDENCE (wisdom): no wisdom.
examples: Their astonishing imprudence shocked everyone.
His imprudence with money left him broke.

meaning: Bold and not showing respect; also (book sense) boldly determined
trick: IMPUDENT - 'im-PRUDENT': speaking without thinking, rudely.
examples: She fought her way with impudent resolve to the front of the crowd.
The impudent boy talked back to his teacher.

meaning: Sudden strong wishes to do something without thinking
trick: IMPULSE - a PULSE that jumps suddenly inside you.
examples: It may be giving in to their own impulses.
Try to control your impulses when shopping.

usage.pattern: act on/resist impulses / an impulse to do something

meaning: Freedom from punishment or bad consequences
trick: IM (no) + PUNI (punish): no punishment.
examples: He seemed reluctant to embrace his friends' air of impunity.
The gang acted with impunity.

meaning: At the last possible moment, only just before it was too late
hindi: ऐन मौके पर, बिल्कुल समय पर
trick: NICK = a tiny cut: you made it with only a tiny cut of time left.
examples: In the nick of time, the Navy's legal department cleared me to proceed.
We reached the station in the nick of time to catch the train.

usage.pattern: do something in the nick of time / arrive in the nick of time
partners: arrive in the nick of time
saved in the nick of time

meaning: A feeling or state of not being good enough
trick: IN (not) + ADEQUACY: not enough.
examples: I must stop surrendering to my feelings of inadequacy.
His inadequacy as a leader became clear.

usage.pattern: feelings of inadequacy / the inadequacy of something

meaning: Not good enough or not enough in amount
trick: IN (not) + ADEQUATE: not enough.
examples: We end up feeling eerily similar to how we started: inadequate.
The food supply was inadequate for the crowd.

meaning: Without meaning to
trick: IN (not) + ADVERT (turn attention): without paying attention.
examples: A stranger might inadvertently offer him a cup of coffee.
I inadvertently deleted the file.

meaning: Formally put (someone) into an important office; also officially opened or started
trick: INAUGURATION day - when presidents are sworn in.
examples: Presidents in Kabul had been inaugurated and murdered.
The minister inaugurated the new hospital.

usage.pattern: be inaugurated as something / inaugurate something

meaning: Without stopping
trick: IN (not) + CEASE: never ceasing.
examples: The children chattered spiritedly and incessantly.
The dog barked incessantly all night.

meaning: Sexual relations between close family members, which is a crime
trick: IN + CEST: 'in the nest' - wrongly within the family.
examples: She worked for years with survivors of incest.
Incest is a crime in most countries.

meaning: Only partly formed or not yet clear
trick: INCHOATE - only an INCH of it made: still unformed.
examples: We act from our deep but invisible and inchoate fears.
He had an inchoate idea for a new business.

meaning: Burning something completely
trick: INCINERATOR - a machine that burns waste to CINDERS.
examples: We were incinerating our own muscle mass for fuel.
The factory is incinerating its waste.

meaning: One of the sharp front teeth used for biting
trick: INCISOR = INCISION (cut): the cutting tooth.
examples: She was ashamed of her yellowing teeth and the missing incisor.
The baby's first incisor appeared at six months.

meaning: To cause or encourage (anger, violence or bad behaviour)
trick: IN + CITE: 'in-sight' of trouble - you stir it up.
examples: Asking "What do you mean?" may incite irritation or defensiveness.
He was arrested for inciting violence.

usage.pattern: incite something / incite someone to do something

meaning: With your real identity hidden
trick: INCOGNITO mode - browse without being recognised.
examples: I preferred to go incognito.
The actor travelled incognito to avoid fans.

meaning: (of speech or thought) not clear and hard to understand
trick: IN (not) + COHERENT: doesn't hang together.
examples: Then came the drowsiness and the incoherent mumbling.
He was so tired his speech became incoherent.

meaning: Not willing or able to believe something
trick: IN (not) + CREDULOUS (believing easily): can't believe it.
examples: He rushed from room to room, furious and incredulous.
She gave an incredulous laugh when she heard the price.

usage.pattern: be incredulous at something / an incredulous + noun

meaning: A hard crust or layer that forms on a surface
trick: IN + CRUST: a crust formed on it.
examples: I pictured every tiny dent or incrustation on the furniture.
There was an incrustation of salt on the old pipe.

meaning: A place or situation that helps something develop; also a machine that keeps babies or eggs warm
trick: INCUBATE eggs - keep them warm so they grow.
examples: My early years were a perfect incubator for stress.
The premature baby was kept in an incubator.

meaning: Necessary as a duty or responsibility (used with on/upon); also currently holding an office
trick: INCUMBENT - 'it's on you': the duty lies on you.
examples: He felt it incumbent upon him to say a few words.
It is incumbent on parents to keep children safe.

usage.pattern: it is incumbent on/upon someone to do something

meaning: Impossible to read or understand
trick: IN (not) + DECIPHER (decode): can't be decoded.
examples: She tried to read his face, but his look was indecipherable.
The doctor's handwriting was indecipherable.

meaning: Never seeming to get tired
trick: IN (not) + DE-FATIGUE: no fatigue ever.
examples: He was indefatigable at this work.
She is an indefatigable campaigner for children's rights.

meaning: Lack of interest or concern
trick: IN (no) + DIFFERENCE: it makes no difference to me.
examples: People imagine a kind of serene indifference to everything.
His indifference to her feelings hurt her.

meaning: Not interested or not caring; also not very good
trick: IN (no) + DIFFERENT: it makes no difference to them.
examples: She couldn't understand how they were so indifferent to the marvels around them.
He seemed indifferent to the result.

meaning: Angry because something seems unfair
trick: IN (not) + DIGN (worthy): angry at being treated as unworthy.
examples: But instead, I was indignant.
She was indignant at being blamed.

meaning: Anger caused by something unfair
trick: IN + DIGNITY hurt: anger when your dignity is attacked.
examples: There was a cry of indignation from everyone.
The new tax caused public indignation.

meaning: Things that make you feel ashamed or lose respect
trick: IN (not) + DIGNITY: things that strip your dignity.
examples: The novel brings home the indignities of war and oppression.
Old people often suffer small indignities in hospitals.

usage.pattern: the indignities of something / suffer indignities

meaning: Not careful about what you say or do, so you draw attention or reveal secrets
trick: IN (not) + DISCREET (careful): not careful.
examples: Talibs patrolled the market looking for the indiscreet laugh.
It was indiscreet of him to tell everyone her secret.

meaning: Without choosing carefully; hitting anyone at random
trick: IN (not) + DISCRIMINATE (choose): not choosing at all.
examples: The militias were killing indiscriminately.
He spends money indiscriminately.

meaning: Taught to accept a set of beliefs without questioning them
trick: IN + DOCTRINE: doctrine pushed into your head.
examples: Many of us have been indoctrinated to be as accepting as possible.
The young soldiers were indoctrinated with hatred.

usage.pattern: be indoctrinated with something / indoctrinate someone

meaning: Not wanting to work or be active
trick: INDOLENT - 'in-dole': lazing on the dole, doing nothing.
examples: It has become something more soft-edged and indolent.
The indolent cat slept all afternoon.

meaning: Impossible to defeat or discourage
trick: IN (not) + DOMIT (tame): can't be tamed.
examples: Mammy was ferocious and indomitable, pacing and ranting.
She showed an indomitable spirit during her illness.

meaning: To let yourself enjoy something, especially too much; also to let someone have what they want
trick: INDULGE - 'in-the-bulge': eat too much and get a bulge.
examples: If you keep indulging in delusional positive thinking, you'll never change.
I like to indulge in ice cream on Sundays.

meaning: Something enjoyable you allow yourself; also being too lenient
trick: INDULGE + -ENCE: the treat you allow yourself.
examples: It was an easily forgivable indulgence.
Chocolate is my one indulgence.

meaning: Not using time, energy or money well
trick: IN (not) + EFFICIENT: wastes effort.
examples: Our brains are inefficient machines.
The old heater is very inefficient.

meaning: Lack of skill or ability
trick: INEPT (clumsy) + -ITUDE: the state of being clumsy.
examples: Once she had found his forgetfulness and ineptitude charming.
The manager's ineptitude cost the company money.

meaning: An unfair situation where people do not have equal rights or chances
trick: IN (not) + EQUALITY: not equal.
examples: The era of nepotism and inequality is over.
Income inequality is growing in many countries.

meaning: Not moving or not able to move
trick: INERT - INERTIA: stays still.
examples: He lay inert on the sofa, too tired to move.
The patient lay inert on the bed.

meaning: Impossible to avoid or ignore
hindi: अनिवार्य, जिससे बचा न जा सके
trick: IN (not) + ESCAPABLE: no escape.
examples: Laila remembered the inescapable drudgery of those four weeks.
The conclusion is inescapable: we need to change.

meaning: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid
trick: IN (not) + EVITABLE (avoidable): can't be avoided.
examples: We must accept the inevitable imperfections of our values.
Change is inevitable.

usage.pattern: it is inevitable that ... / the inevitable + noun

meaning: Impossible to stop or change
trick: IN (not) + EXORABLE (can be pleaded with): no pleading stops it.
examples: Chance had once played a happy part in that inexorable march of events.
Nothing could slow the inexorable rise in prices.

meaning: Impossible to explain or understand
trick: IN (not) + EXPLICABLE: can't be explained.
examples: My body crouches, protecting itself against something imagined and inexplicable.
For some inexplicable reason, the lights went out.

usage.pattern: an inexplicable + noun / it is inexplicable that ...

meaning: Too strong or deep to be put into words
trick: IN (not) + EXPRESS + IBLE: cannot be expressed.
examples: Gusts of an inexpressible blackness kept passing through Mariam.
She felt an inexpressible joy when her son came home.

meaning: So closely linked that it cannot be separated or pulled apart
trick: IN (not) + EXTRICATE (set free): you can't free it from the knot.
examples: Pain is an inextricable thread in the fabric of life.
Music is an inextricable part of our festivals.

usage.pattern: be inextricable from something / an inextricable + noun

meaning: The time when someone is a baby or very young child; also the very early stage of something
trick: INFANT + -CY: the time when you're an infant.
examples: I had known that tune in my infancy, but I had long forgotten it.
My grandmother has looked after me since infancy.

usage.pattern: in someone's infancy / in its infancy / from infancy

meaning: The crime of killing a baby or young child
trick: INFANT + -CIDE (killing, as in pesticide).
examples: It was being put about that the animals were dying of famine and had resorted to infanticide.
Infanticide is a serious crime in every country.

usage.pattern: commit infanticide / the practice of infanticide

meaning: A large, very hot fire that is out of control; also a place or situation like hell
trick: Dante's INFERNO = the fire of hell.
examples: Buffalo had been like living in a blazing inferno.
The old wooden house became an inferno within minutes.

usage.pattern: a blazing inferno / turn into an inferno

meaning: A large number of insects or animals living in a place and causing damage or disease
trick: INFEST: pests holding a FEST in your house.
examples: It was the worst cockroach infestation I ever saw on the job.
The kitchen had an ant infestation after the rains.

usage.pattern: an infestation of something / a + pest + infestation

meaning: People who do not believe in a particular religion (offensive, used by some believers)
trick: IN (not) + FIDEL (faithful, as in fidelity): not of the faith.
examples: The extremists called everyone outside their faith infidels.
In old stories, crusaders and their enemies called each other infidels.

usage.pattern: call someone infidels / fight the infidels

meaning: Weakness or illness, especially caused by old age
trick: IN (not) + FIRM: the body is not firm any more.
examples: I couldn't decide if they were greeting me or if it was some infirmity of age.
Despite her infirmity, grandma still walks to the temple.

usage.pattern: the infirmity of age / suffer from an infirmity

meaning: A part of the body that becomes red, swollen, hot and painful, often from injury or infection
trick: IN + FLAME: the body part feels as if it's on fire.
examples: I had so much inflammation that the slightest movement hurt.
The doctor gave him medicine to reduce the inflammation in his knee.

meaning: Causing something unpleasant, such as damage, pain or suffering, to someone
trick: INFLICT ~ 'in-flick': flicking a whip IN on someone.
examples: Learn how to handle conflict without inflicting damage.
The storm passed without inflicting much harm on the village.

usage.pattern: inflict something on someone / without inflicting something

meaning: An act of breaking a rule or law, usually a minor one
trick: IN + FRACTION: a small FRACTURE (break) of a rule.
examples: I served nearly twenty years without a single infraction on my record.
Parking in the wrong spot is a minor infraction.

usage.pattern: an infraction of something (a rule or law)

meaning: To make someone extremely angry
trick: IN + FURY: puts fury into someone.
examples: There was always some minor thing that would infuriate him.
Loud phone calls on the bus infuriate my mother.

usage.pattern: something infuriates someone / it infuriates someone that...

meaning: Making you extremely angry or annoyed
trick: FURY inside: it fills you with fury.
examples: The boss had an infuriating habit of dropping by with urgent, poorly planned work.
Waiting an hour for a late bus is infuriating.

usage.pattern: be infuriating / an infuriating + noun / it is infuriating that...

meaning: Filled something with a quality or feeling so it spreads all through it; also soaked herbs in liquid for flavour
trick: IN + FUSED: fused into everything.
examples: My years of negotiating had infused everything, even my parenting style.
Her speech infused the team with new hope.

usage.pattern: infuse something with something / infuse something into something

meaning: Being innocent, trusting and honest, sometimes too much so
trick: INGENUOUS (naive) is not INGENIOUS (clever): the extra U = 'U trust everyone'.
examples: The Prosecutor said he was amazed at his friend's ingenuousness.
The child's ingenuousness made everyone smile.

meaning: Taken food, drink or medicine into the body by swallowing
trick: IN + GEST (carry, as in digest): carried into the body.
examples: Once ingested, your body will wake up feeling more alive.
The dog was sick after it ingested chocolate.

meaning: To live in a place
trick: IN + HABITat: your habitat is where you inhabit.
examples: England could feed far more animals than now inhabit it.
Tigers inhabit the forests of central India.

meaning: Being a basic, natural part of something that cannot be removed
trick: IN + HERE: it's always here, inside it.
examples: Dissatisfaction and unease are inherent parts of human nature.
There is an inherent risk in any business.

usage.pattern: be inherent in something / an inherent + noun

meaning: Too shy or nervous to express your feelings or act freely
trick: IN + HIBIT ~ 'hide a bit': you hold yourself back.
examples: Before the tragedy, I was inhibited and obsessed with what others thought of me.
He feels inhibited when speaking in front of a big crowd.

meaning: Informal: mentions or articles in newspapers and magazines; also coloured liquid for writing or printing
trick: Newspapers are printed in INK, so 'good ink' = good press.
examples: I booked more positive ink for the SEALs in magazines.
The new film got a lot of ink in the local papers.

usage.pattern: get ink / positive ink for someone

meaning: A small pot that holds ink for dipping a pen; used to describe something deep black
trick: INK + WELL: a little well full of ink.
examples: All I could see were lights streaking like comets in an inkwell sky.
My grandfather's old desk still has a brass inkwell.

usage.pattern: an inkwell / dip a pen in the inkwell

meaning: Very dark or black, like ink
trick: INK + Y: as black as ink.
examples: Huge plumes of inky exhaust choked from the tail pipe.
We looked up at the inky night sky.

meaning: A person kept in a prison; also someone living in a hospital or care home
trick: IN + MATE: your mate on the INside of jail.
examples: If an officer approaches an inmate expecting him to resist, he often will.
The inmate was released after ten years.

meaning: People kept in a prison; also people living in a hospital or care home
trick: IN + MATES: mates on the INside of jail.
examples: This was where inmates met visitors.
The inmates eat lunch together at noon.

meaning: A small hotel or pub, often in the countryside, where travellers can eat and stay
trick: Go IN to the INN for the night.
examples: He left his wife and child in another inn.
We stayed at a cosy inn near the mountains.

meaning: Present in you from birth, not learned
trick: IN + NATE (natal = birth): in you since birth.
examples: All the meaning in our life is shaped by this innate desire to never truly die.
She has an innate talent for music.

usage.pattern: an innate + noun / be innate in someone

meaning: Not harmful or offensive
trick: IN (not) + NOC (harm, as in noxious): not harmful.
examples: Those innocuous words bubbled up in our minds each time a wave pulled us under.
It was an innocuous question, but she got upset.

meaning: Eager to know or ask questions; curious
trick: INQUISitive ~ INQUIre: always inquiring.
examples: She repeated his words in an inquisitive tone.
Inquisitive children ask 'why' all day.

usage.pattern: be inquisitive about something / an inquisitive + noun

meaning: Extreme foolishness; also serious mental illness
trick: IN (not) + SANE: not sane.
examples: Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different result.
Driving that fast in the rain is pure insanity.

usage.pattern: it is insanity to do something

meaning: Written or carved on a surface, especially so it lasts
trick: IN + SCRIBE (write): written into it.
examples: FOUR LEGS GOOD, TWO LEGS BAD was inscribed on the end wall of the barn.
Her name was inscribed on the trophy.

usage.pattern: be inscribed on something / be inscribed with something

meaning: Spreading harm slowly and secretly, so you hardly notice it
trick: INSIDE + IOUS: harm creeping inside you.
examples: There's an insidious quirk to your brain that can drive you batty.
Sugar addiction is insidious because it starts so small.

meaning: Not really meaning what you say or do; pretending
trick: IN (not) + SINCERE.
examples: His apologies had been halfhearted and insincere.
Her smile looked insincere.

meaning: Pretending to feel or mean something that you do not
trick: IN (not) + SINCERITY: no sincerity inside.
examples: She could hear the insincerity that had always lurked beneath his words.
I could sense the insincerity in his praise.

usage.pattern: the insincerity of something / insincerity in someone's voice

meaning: To suggest something unpleasant in an indirect way
trick: IN + SIN-uate: hinting that someone has SINned.
examples: They seemed to insinuate that the other side was being dishonest.
Are you trying to insinuate that I lied?

meaning: Suggesting or creating something in a quiet, indirect way; also hinting at something unpleasant
trick: IN + SIN-uate: slipping an idea in quietly.
examples: Mirroring is the art of insinuating similarity.
He kept insinuating that I was late on purpose.

meaning: Firmly demanding or saying that something must happen
trick: INSIST + ENCE: the act of insisting.
examples: At her insistence, Jalil described the cinema to her.
At my mother's insistence, I took an umbrella.

usage.pattern: at someone's insistence / insistence on something

meaning: Continuing for a long time and hard to ignore; also firmly demanding something
trick: INSIST-ENT: it keeps insisting.
examples: He complained about the baby's insistent crying.
The insistent ringing of the phone woke me up.

usage.pattern: an insistent + noun / be insistent on something / be insistent that...

meaning: Impossible to solve or explain; also unable to dissolve in liquid
hindi: असमाधेय, जिसका हल न हो; अघुलनशील
trick: IN (not) + SOLUBLE (solvable): no solution.
examples: The animals found the problem insoluble.
It seemed an insoluble puzzle until my brother helped.

usage.pattern: an insoluble problem / find something insoluble

meaning: In a natural way, without thinking or learning
hindi: स्वाभाविक रूप से, सहज रूप से
trick: INSTINCT + UALLY: done by instinct.
examples: Because we are apes, we instinctually measure ourselves against others.
The baby instinctually reached for her mother.

meaning: Protected or separated from something outside, such as noise, cold or people
trick: INSULA = island (Latin): kept like an island, cut off.
examples: Mariam sat in the corner, insulated by a wall of steam.
The house is well insulated against the cold.

usage.pattern: be insulated from/against something / insulated by something

meaning: Covering something to protect it from heat, cold, electricity or noise
trick: INSULA (island): making it an island safe from heat.
examples: The foam formed around my hands, insulating them from the hot metal.
Wool is good at insulating the body from cold.

meaning: An armed fight by a group against the government
trick: IN + SURGE: rebels surging up against the rulers.
examples: They were dealing with an Islamist insurgency in South Thailand.
The army struggled to control the insurgency in the hills.

usage.pattern: an insurgency against someone / fight an insurgency

meaning: Fighting against the government or those in power; also a rebel fighter
trick: IN + SURGE: surging up against the rulers.
examples: She saw pamphlets from insurgent groups headquartered in Pakistan.
The insurgent leaders agreed to peace talks.

meaning: Too big or difficult to deal with or overcome
trick: IN (not) + SURMOUNT (climb over): a mountain you can't climb.
examples: I knew the pain would become unbearable and feel insurmountable.
The problem seemed insurmountable, but we solved it together.

meaning: Being honest and having strong moral principles
trick: INTEGER = whole number: a person of integrity is whole, not broken by lies.
examples: He taught me the values of hard work and integrity.
Our teacher is a woman of great integrity.

usage.pattern: a person of integrity / have integrity

meaning: Informal: useful information, especially secret or military information
trick: Short for INTELligence.
examples: This time, I had that intel going in.
Do you have any intel on the new manager?

usage.pattern: have intel on something / get intel

meaning: Made something stronger or more extreme; also became stronger
trick: INTENSE + -IFIED: made more intense.
examples: Each drop of his spit burned like venom and intensified my hate.
The rain intensified in the evening.

meaning: Getting involved in something when you are not wanted
trick: INTER (between) + FERE: someone getting in between.
examples: Now the plan could go forward without his interference.
She wanted to study without any interference from her family.

usage.pattern: interference in/with something / interference from someone

meaning: Extremely high or huge (informal, figurative); also between galaxies in space
hindi: आसमान छूती, बहुत ऊँची; आकाशगंगाओं के बीच
trick: INTER (between) + GALACTIC: reaching as far as the galaxies.
examples: I knew the moment had arrived, and my expectations were intergalactic.
Her dreams for her son were intergalactic.

meaning: For a short time only, until something permanent is arranged
trick: INTERIM = IN the meanTIME.
examples: The country has an interim president now, Hamid Karzai.
He will be the interim captain until the coach picks a new one.

usage.pattern: an interim + noun / in the interim

meaning: Said something suddenly, interrupting someone
trick: INTER (between) + JECT (throw): threw words in between.
examples: After three minutes, Gabriella Blum interjected.
"That's not true," my brother interjected.

meaning: Mixed or woven together with something else
trick: INTER + LACE: laces woven between each other.
examples: It was a strange pleasure, interlaced with the pain.
Her story was interlaced with funny moments.

meaning: A short period between two longer events, different from them
trick: INTER (between) + LUDE (play): a little play between the acts.
examples: All of it seemed like a dream, a mere interlude between that afternoon and this moment.
We had a brief interlude of sunshine between the storms.

usage.pattern: an interlude between something and something

meaning: Closely joined or connected with something, like twisted threads
trick: INTER + TWINE (string): strings twisted together.
examples: Our governor is buried deep in our minds, intertwined with our very identity.
Their lives became intertwined after they married.

meaning: A planned talk where people confront someone about a problem to help them; also the act of stepping in to change a situation
trick: INTER (between) + VENE (come): coming in between.
examples: What started as a venting session had become a solo intervention.
Quick intervention by the doctors saved his life.

usage.pattern: an intervention in something / stage an intervention

meaning: Very personal and private; also very close and friendly
trick: INTIMATE ~ 'inner-mate': only your inner circle sees it.
examples: In a rare intimate interview, Mustaine admitted he still felt like a failure.
She shared intimate details of her childhood.

usage.pattern: an intimate + noun / be intimate with someone

meaning: The rises and falls of the voice when speaking
trick: IN + TONE: the tones in your voice.
examples: Laila marveled at her daughter's thoughtful pauses and intonations.
Learning the right intonations makes your English sound natural.

meaning: In a very detailed and complicated way
trick: INTRICATE ~ 'in-tricky': many tricky little parts.
examples: His neck looked too thin to support the intricately wrapped turban.
The temple doors are intricately carved.

meaning: Secret plans to harm someone or gain power; also interest or curiosity
trick: INTRIGUE ~ 'in-trick': tricks planned in secret.
examples: It is a heartfelt saga of romance, war and political intrigue.
The old palace was full of intrigue and gossip.

usage.pattern: intrigue against someone / a web of intrigue

meaning: Very interested and curious about something
trick: INTRIGUED ~ 'in-tricked': tricked into wanting to know more.
examples: They told him about the SEALs, and he was intrigued.
I was intrigued by the strange old map.

usage.pattern: be intrigued by something / intrigued to know

meaning: Entering or interrupting where you are not wanted
trick: IN + TRUDE (push): pushing in.
examples: Rasheed looked up with displeasure at the unwelcome intrusion.
Sorry for the intrusion, but dinner is ready.

meaning: A huge amount of something arriving at once, too much to deal with; also a flood of water
trick: UNDA = wave (Latin): waves pouring IN.
examples: The inundation of the exceptional makes people feel worse about themselves.
After the sale, the shop faced an inundation of orders.

meaning: Always, every single time
trick: IN (not) + VARY: it never varies.
examples: Bibi jo was invariably accompanied by one of her six brides.
He invariably arrives five minutes late.

usage.pattern: invariably do something / be invariably + adjective

meaning: An army entering another country to take control of it; also an unwanted entry
trick: IN + VADE (go): going in by force.
examples: We were in a bowling alley when we watched the invasion of Iraq.
Many families fled after the invasion.

usage.pattern: an invasion of a place / launch an invasion

meaning: Good at thinking of new and original ideas
trick: INVENT + IVE: always inventing.
examples: Snowball was quicker in speech and more inventive than Napoleon.
She is very inventive in the kitchen.

meaning: Making you feel full of energy and fresh
trick: VIGOR inside: it puts vigour (energy) into you.
examples: The right problems should be invigorating you and motivating you.
A cold shower in the morning is invigorating.

meaning: Too strong to be defeated or hurt
trick: IN (not) + VINC (conquer): cannot be conquered.
examples: Once you are comfortable with life's hardships, you become invincible.
The team felt invincible after ten straight wins.

meaning: A tall plant with large blue, purple or yellow flowers; also the coloured part of the eye
hindi: आइरिस का फूल; आँख का रंगीन भाग
trick: IRIS was the Greek rainbow goddess: rainbow-coloured flowers and eyes.
examples: The grassy banks were sprinkled with blue-lavender wild iris.
She planted purple iris along the garden path.

usage.pattern: wild iris / a bunch of irises

meaning: Slightly annoying or irritating
trick: IRK = irritate; IRKsome = some irritation.
examples: One thing in those early days was really irksome: my habit of thinking like a free man.
Waiting in long queues is irksome.

usage.pattern: be irksome (to someone) / an irksome + noun

meaning: Too strong or lively to be held back or controlled
hindi: अदम्य, जो रोका न जा सके
trick: IR (not) + REPRESS (hold down): can't be held down.
examples: And yet the song was irrepressible.
Her irrepressible laughter filled the room.

meaning: In a way that cannot be changed or undone
hindi: अपरिवर्तनीय रूप से, हमेशा के लिए
trick: IR (not) + REVOKE (take back): can't be taken back.
examples: I was caught in the rattrap irrevocably.
Their friendship was irrevocably damaged after the fight.

meaning: Supplying water to land or crops through channels or pipes
trick: IRRIGATE ~ 'open the GATE': let water into the fields.
examples: The fields were crisscrossed by streams and irrigation ditches.
Farmers here depend on canal irrigation.

meaning: Islands, especially small ones (used in poems and names)
trick: ISLE = ISLand without the 'and'.
examples: Thousands of Japanese soldiers were still scattered among the Pacific isles.
We sailed past green isles on our holiday.

usage.pattern: the + name + Isles / among the isles

meaning: Separate and happening only here and there; also alone and cut off from others
trick: ISOLA = island (Italian): like islands, standing apart.
examples: Only some of his gestures caught my attention, but these were isolated patches.
There were only isolated showers this afternoon.

usage.pattern: isolated + noun / be isolated from something

meaning: Copying another person's body language or behaviour (a formal word for mirroring)
trick: ISO (same) + PRAXIS (action): doing the same action.
examples: Mirroring, also called isopraxism, is essentially imitation.
Close friends often show isopraxism by sitting the same way.
